slides.title: In 1972, France found uranium that had already been used.

slides.body:
At a French nuclear fuel plant, a routine check on ore from Oklo, in Gabon, found 0.717% uranium-235.

Everywhere else, in Earth's crust, on the Moon, even in meteorites, the figure is 0.720%.

In part of the mine, the shortfall added up to about 200 kg of uranium-235. Enough for several bombs.

Nothing had been stolen. Investigators traced the missing atoms back to the rock itself.

slides.kicker: The mine had been a reactor.
slides.body:
Two billion years ago, natural uranium held about 3% uranium-235, close to modern reactor fuel.

When groundwater seeped into the ore, it slowed the neutrons just enough. A chain reaction started. On its own.

slides.kicker: It switched itself on and off.
slides.body: Roughly every three hours. In some zones, for more than 150,000 years.

slides.kicker: One scientist had seen it coming.
slides.body:
In 1956, Paul Kuroda calculated that a natural reactor was possible. Few took the idea seriously.

Oklo proved him right. Today its rocks help scientists study how nuclear waste moves underground.

slides.lead: When a number is slightly off, it's tempting to round it away.
slides.accent: Sometimes the anomaly is the discovery.

slides.line: Save this for the next time a result looks wrong.

caption:
In 1972, a routine check found uranium that was missing a tiny bit of its fuel. The explanation: the mine in Gabon had run as a natural nuclear reactor, two billion years ago. ☢️

The smallest anomaly can hide the biggest story.

Have you ever ignored a small detail that turned out to matter?
